en: Homage to the Protector, the Sage, who is a mass of inconceivable, marvelous, and unafflicted wisdom and dispassion,
and who is an unfathomable ocean of devotion to the Blessed One.
Salutations to him, whose greatness in the excellence of his passion for the knowledge of the reality of the lotus-feet of the Conqueror of Madhu reaches its ultimate limit;
to Nātha Muni, the Protector, whose feet are my eternal refuge both in this world and the next. YStr_2 //

Again, homage to the Lord Sage, the best among those who practice self-restraint, who has descended into the world through the yoga of complete devotion to the ultimate truth, and whose auspicious words are like a surging flood from the ocean of the nectar of knowledge regarding the reality of boundless, unwavering devotion.

Salutations to that sage Parāśara, the illustrious one, who in ancient times fashioned this jewel of a Purāṇa, clearly demonstrating in its true essence the nature of the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord, as well as their respective states of existence, enjoyment, liberation, and the means thereto.
Mother, father, young women, sons, wealth— whatever belongs to my lineage by right—
I bow my head to that glorious pair of feet of our primal family lord, which are as delightful as the *vakula* flower.

I shall praise that lotus-foot of the lotus-eyed Lord, which shines upon my head and in the crests of the Vedas, and into which the entire path of our heart's desires converges— that which is the family treasure and the tutelary deity of our lineage.

Salutations to that shameless poet who attempts to compose a hymn to His majesty— he whose ocean of greatness cannot be measured even by its droplets by Śarva, Pitāmaha, and the others in their true essence.
Or rather, I praise you thus until exhaustion or according to my capacity, for even they—
the Vedas and the faces of the four-faced Brahmā—
praise you constantly; yet what difference is there between a mustard seed and Mount Kula (Meru) when both are submerged within the great ocean?
Moreover, O Lotus-eyed One, this worshiper is not to be pitied by you because of his superior power, but rather because of the exhaustion incurred by the act of praise;
for such exhaustion is easily obtained by one of dull intellect like me, and thus this exertion is appropriate for me.

If You did not take heed of these worlds, O Lord, they would not even be able to exist; how then could there be their continued activity? Thus, O Master, while You are a natural friend to all living beings, this affection for those who have sought refuge in You is truly wonderful.
O Nārāyaṇa, what follower of the Vedas would not acknowledge your inherent and unsurpassed sovereignty?
For even Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and the supreme sovereign [Viṣṇu] are but mere droplets from the ocean of your majesty.
Who is Śrī?
Who is the supreme refuge for all beings?
Who is the lotus-eyed one?
Who is the Supreme Person?

In what infinitesimal fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a ten-thousandth part of whom does the universe exist, with its diverse manifestations of consciousness and matter? (Yoga Sūtra-bhāṣya 1.24)

Who else besides Prajāpati and Paśupati bestows the greatest fruits by liberating one from the sins of stealing the Vedas, the heavy transgressions against gurus, and the afflictions caused by demons?
And whose water from the feet does Śiva bear upon his own head?
In whose womb is this manifold universe, headed by Hara and Viriñca?
Who protects it? And from whose navel was it born?
Who other than you could swallow [the world] after traversing it and then vomit it up again?
By whom, indeed, can it be suspected that he is dependent on another? // YStr_14 //
Because of your conduct, character, and deeds; because of your supreme excellence of being, your virtuous nature, and your mastery of powerful scriptures;
and because of the opinions of those who know the supreme truth of destiny—you cannot be understood by those of demonic nature.

Some who possess no other devotion than for you behold incessantly your own nature of expansive greatness— surpassing all estimation and transcending the threefold limits— even as it is being concealed by you through the power of illusion.
The cosmic egg and that which lies within the interior of the egg, the ten successive coverings, the qualities (guṇas),
primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual soul (puruṣa), the supreme state, and the Brahman beyond the highest— these are Your manifestations.
Self-controlled, generous, virtuous, upright, pure, gentle, compassionate, sweet, steadfast,
even-minded, skillful, and grateful— you too are by nature an ocean of the nectar of all auspicious qualities.

Even those who, proceeding in succession, imagine hundreds of Puruṣas each higher than the lotus-born Brahmā, remain forever occupied with the desire to reach the ocean of even one of Your qualities; they do not excel You through their effort.

For those who have taken refuge in you, the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, as well as liberation from saṃsāra, become mere playful pastimes; these Vedic functions follow the profound mind of yours.
Homage, homage to you who transcend the realms of speech and mind; homage, homage to you whose sole realm is speech and mind.
Homage, homage to you of infinite and great majesty; homage, homage to you whose singular intention is infinite compassion.
I am not established in the Dharma, nor am I a knower of the Self,
nor do I possess devotion for the lotus-feet of Your feet.
Possessing nothing and having no other resort, O Refuge,
I take refuge at the soles of your feet.
There is no action in this world, even by the thousands, that has not been performed by me.
Yet here I am, O Mukunda, at the moment of its ripening;
now I cry out before you, having no other refuge.
O Infinite One,
as I was sinking within the depths of the ocean of existence, you have finally been found by me like a shore;
and now, O Blessed One, you too have found this unsurpassed vessel of compassion.
What has never happened before will now happen to me, for all suffering is innate to me; yet,
O Protector, this defeat of those who have come to you for refuge before you is not worthy of you.
O Great Lord, even though I am rejected, I do not yet venture to abandon your lotus feet;
for even an infant, though cast out in anger while still nursing at the breast, never desires to leave its mother’s feet.
How could one who has fixed his soul upon your lotus-feet, which distill the flow of nectar, desire anything else?
For when a lotus abounds with honey, the bee does not look toward the thorny kṣuraka plant.
If, with your feet as the sole object in mind, someone ever offers a single joined palm— even once, in whatever manner—
then at that very moment it utterly steals away all inauspiciousness, nourishes all that is auspicious, and never diminishes.
The spray from the ocean of nectar that is devotion to Your pair of reddish lotus-feet extinguishes in an instant the raging forest fire of saṃsāra and bestows supreme bliss.

When shall I behold with my own eyes your lotus-feet—the abode of playful prowess, the supreme refuge for those who have transcended the world, and which finds its moment of leisure in dispelling the suffering of those who bow before you? May I obtain my wealth [in the form of that vision]! // YStr_30 //
But when, O Trivikrama, will Your pair of lotus feet— marked with the conch, the discus, the mace, the banner, the lotus, the goad, and the thunderbolt— adorn my head? (Yoga Sūtra Commentary 31)
He was resplendent, clothed in brilliant yellow garments, with a pure complexion like a smiling *atasī* flower;
his navel was deep-set, his waist slender, and he was tall, possessing the marks that beautify the expanse of his broad chest.
He shone with his four beautiful arms, which reached down to his knees and were roughened by the calluses of the bowstring,
proclaiming the pressing of his beloved’s ear-ornaments of blue lotuses and the loosening of her braided hair.
With high, fleshy shoulders, with earrings hanging down, and with a neck made beautiful by a row of locks of hair and a conch-like throat;
with the splendor of his face surpassing the full, stainless orb of the moon and the radiant beauty of a lotus.
With beautiful eyes like blossoming lotuses, playful creeper-like eyebrows,
radiant lips, a pure smile, tender cheeks, a prominent nose, and locks of hair hanging down to his forehead— YStr_35.
Resplendent with a trembling crown, armlets, necklaces, a jeweled necklace, a girdle-string, anklets, and other ornaments;
and shining with the excellent discus, conch, sword, mace, and bow, as well as a garland of forest *tulasī*.
You have made her whose abode is your embrace, whose birthplace is your beloved home,
upon whom the entire world depends through the grace of your sidelong glances, and for whose sake the ocean was churned and bound.
By Your own sovereign splendor— which, though ever-experienced, produces wonder as if it were something unprecedented—
by Your excellence, Your form, and Your graceful gestures, which are eternally suited only to You, [O Śrī].

Seated together with her upon the serpent Ananta, the sole abode of the power of supreme wisdom, whose divine splendor within his belly is illuminated by the circles of rays from the multitude of jewels on his hoods; YS 39.

When people say, "May you have [these things]," as you pass into the state of being a remnant through various bodily forms—such as dwellings, beds, seats, sandals, garments, pillows, and protection against rain and sun—[you fulfill their wishes] accordingly. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.30)
Your servant, friend, vehicle, seat, banner, canopy, and fan—all composed of the three Vedas—is Garuda, who stands before You;
he is beautiful with the scar on his shoulder caused by the friction of Your feet.
As you, who had entrusted the burden of your own self to your beloved general— who subsisted on the remnants of what you had eaten—
reported each matter exactly as it was, you granted your assent with noble glances.
He is being served appropriately by ministers who, having destroyed all stains of affliction, are by nature of a single flavor with your favor,
are worthy of you, and have assumed their respective roles as attendants and instruments.

With his great arms, he delighted the Queen with a playful charm that was both innocent and refined— a charm composed of a continuous flow of unprecedented and manifold aesthetic sentiments, which in a mere moment could cast aside the vastness of time from the beginning of the world.
[He is] an ocean of the nectar of beauty, whose nature is inconceivable, divine, marvelous, and eternally youthful;
the glory of Śrī, the sole life of his devotees, the capable friend in adversity, and the wish-fulfilling tree for those in need.
Constantly following the Blessed One alone, with all other desires entirely stilled,
when shall I, as his exclusive and eternal servant, gladden him, my life having found its true protector?

Fie on me—impure, undisciplined, fearless, and shameless, O Supreme Person! For I, acting according to my own desires, long for the status of being Your attendant, a position that is utterly beyond the reach of even the foremost among the best of yogis, such as Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sanaka, and others.

O Hari, you who are the vessel for a thousand offenses, please, out of pure compassion, take into yourself this wretched one who has fallen into the belly of the terrifying ocean of existence and has come to you for refuge.

O Blessed One, look with compassion upon me who have stumbled on the path in this storm of worldly existence, where the quarters of the sky are blinded by the thick darkness of lack of discrimination and which rains down manifold, incessant suffering.
This request of mine is not false; listen to my single petition before you.
O Lord, if you do not show me mercy, then one more worthy of your compassion than I will be difficult for you to find.
Therefore, without you I have no protector, and without me you would be pitiable;
O Blessed One, do not abandon this lineage ordained by fate.
Whatever I may be, by virtue of my body or other qualities, in whatever manner I exist—
such as I am, I offer myself this very day at your lotus feet.
O my Lord Mādhava, whatever I possess and whoever I am—all that is indeed yours alone;
since my awakened intellect realizes this is my fixed nature, what more, then, should I offer to you?
O Blessed One, since You Yourself have made me realize this eternal devotion of Yours toward me through Your very compassion, likewise grant me that devotion which is not to be enjoyed by any other.
May I even take birth as an insect in your palaces, which are the sole abode of the happiness of servitude;
but may I never have birth, even with the nature of the four-faced Brahmā, in the dwellings of others.

May those great-souled ones, who have treated even unsurpassed worldly enjoyment and liberation as mere straw out of the desire to behold your form even once, look upon me; lead me [there], for separation from you is unbearable even for a single moment.

Neither my body, nor my life-breaths, nor every desired pleasure, nor even myself, nor anything else whatsoever—O Lord, I cannot endure it as something external to you for even a moment due to the majesty of your being my remainder; may that [endurance] perish a hundredfold. This is my true petition, O Slayer of Madhu.

O Ocean of Compassion, O Friend, O Sea of Boundless Affection, though I am a beast among men, a locus of evil, and a repository of great, endless, beginningless, and unavoidable misfortune, I desire to be free from fear by repeatedly recollecting the multitude of Your virtues.
Even though I did not desire this, as if I did— having composed these deceptive verses of praise while shrouded by passion and ignorance—
even so, O Supporter of the Earth, out of compassion please instruct my mind, which has become thus, by relying upon such words as these.
You are the father, you are the mother, you are the beloved son, you are the dear friend; you alone are the teacher and you are the refuge of the worlds.
I am yours, your servant, your attendant, and one who has found his way to you; since I have thus sought refuge, I am indeed your very burden to bear.

Having been born into a great lineage in this world of those renowned for their fame— lineage that is pure, disciplined, and possessed of those who know the reality of the principles of the qualities and the person—
I, a sinful soul, O Giver of Refuge, sink lower and lower into darkness by my very nature, while your lotus feet are the sole object of the minds of those whose hearts are devoted to them.
Boundless, base, fickle-minded, a source of malice, ungrateful, arrogant, enslaved by passion, intent on deception,
cruel, and most sinful— how could I, such as I am, cross over this shoreless ocean of suffering to serve at your two feet?

O best of the Raghus, that you were so compassionate toward the crow who bowed before you; O Kṛṣṇa, that you granted liberation to the foolish Caidya despite his offenses in every birth—tell me, what transgression was there for which you were not capable of forgiveness?
Surely I have already surrendered to you, O Lord, and am entreating you, saying, "I am yours.
You ought to show me compassion and remember your promises; why then is this your vow, excluding me alone?
